utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we don't hear Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, yes, I can hear you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're hearing now, I suppose, Mr. Brdjanin because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's the interpreter who didn't hear Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's no longer a problem. Thank you, Mr. Brdjanin. Good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's going to be one of those days, Your Honour. I was pressing the wrong button. Joanna Korner, Timothy Resch together with Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you three. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, together with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to the three of you. Let's start, assuming that there are no preliminaries. Usher, could you please bring the witness in, thank you. Do you think you'll finish with the witness today Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do. With always the caveat that I'm so often wrong when it comes to the documents, but I do think I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning to you, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you kindly make the solemn declaration once more, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Thank you. Ms. Korner will be proceeding with her in chief. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, good morning.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we carry on looking at your reports, there is one question I want to ask you in respect to the refugees. Apart from the Muslim refugees that we have been looking at, were there also Serb refugees that you were having to deal with, who were coming from the parts of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a point that is a little salient, difficult to see. There were indeed refugees crossing or displaced persons crossing the Bosnian border into the sector where the UN was deployed but when it came to Serbs, this was never really an issue because the Serbs would tell us ex post facto that we have refugees here, you didn't even know it or you didn't raise the international awareness that you do with non-Serbs, but what happened was that they took care of it themselves, that -- without the usual distress that is accompanied by refugees who were non-Serbs crossing that border into hostile reception from the opposite side. With the Serbs, there was no hostility when they crossed the border and because there were a number of empty houses so to speak, there would be quietly accommodated without us knowing exactly who is where. That's the -- why the issue looks deceptively silent. That's how this point has been raised elsewhere, why were we not so occupied with the Serbs? Not so. That's because of the way it was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So to summarise that, the Serbs who were coming into your area were being housed by other Serbs and were not facing, as you put it, a hostile reception?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And indeed, as I understand your evidence, quite often they would be taken in without your even being aware of the fact that there were refugees?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right could you now have a look, please, at a whole bundle? It's P1669, because it's a whole collection of reports that you forwarded to your superiors, I think. Dated the 29th of June. We see on the top there, your covering letter. It's actually, subject, Mr. Suad -- is that Adilovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's somebody else's handwriting. I would have to look at the printed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay, don't worry then. And then you say, "Please find the blank page memo and annexes, I think it's one page memo and annexes total 18 pages on the above-mentioned subject." Now, if we look at the typed copy which is the memorandum, dated the 29th of June, subject, Mr. Suad Adilovic's letter?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I refer to your message of the 26th of June, the story of Bosanski Novi and other flash points on the Bosnia-Herzegovina border is a heartbreaking tale of violence and unconfirmed atrocities in the making. We have made a series of reports on this subject and enclose the following which may give you a sense of our frustration with the situation. And signed by you and the reports are listed. Addressed to Mr. Mick Magnusson, UNPROFOR Zagreb. Mr. Magnusson being whom?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an assistant directly in the office next to Mr. Cedric Thornberry and Mr. Cedric Thornberry had tasked him to pursue the matter with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at the next document which is the 22nd of June of 1992. Group of people held at football stadium, Bosanski Novi, DanCon informs civil affairs of a fresh group of about 15 persons apparently being held in the football stadium and being guarded by people in camouflage uniforms. The people waved white flags and flashed SOS signals to passing DanCon patrol. Then please find attached a letter addressed to the mayor of Bosanski Novi by the UNHCR representative here in Topusko. This letter particularly the 5th paragraph is designed to reinforce a message that has repeatedly been orally conveyed to him and to his colleagues in Dvor, best regards. Now can we deal with the first paragraph? This is the Danish -- I don't know what Con stands for, the Danish contingent, that's it, reporting to you or to your office that there are more people in the Bosanski Novi football stadium. This business of SOS signals, what exactly was happening there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, to understand it a little bit of the relationship between that football field and where the Danish contingent was. It's a direct line of vision relationship. Their contingent, the Danish contingent located in Dvor, from their observation tower, you can see directly across the river into the football field in the direction of Bosanski Novi, and that of course the reverse is true, if you're on the other side, you can see the Danish observation point. Since this, as you noted in the earlier memorandum you read, introducing this package, that we speak about talking about this matter in previous report, and this is related to the paragraph, this fresh number of people coming in here. There was a constant flow of people into that football field. Military observers in Dvor, with their binoculars could see what was going on there and on this occasion, there was a formation of SOS from those people in that football field and you can see, and you can draw the conclusion they intended to be seen. The people making that SOS intended that they be seen across.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you said the formation of SOS. You mean they were standing so that the letters SOS could be seen?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the report said from the military observers themselves is that we read a formation, how the military exactly read it, I couldn't tell you exactly but they say we can see, we the soldiers, that formation made up of human beings and flags spells SOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think just for a moment, can we have back the map, the big map that we produced? I've forgotten -- it's the coloured one, I've forgotten the exhibit number, P1645. Just so we can remind ourselves of where Dvor and Bosanski Novi were. I think we can see fairly clearly, well Bosanski Novi is marked heavily, it's just over the border and over the river, and then Dvor is just there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, thank you very much. Usher, you can take that away now. If we go on please, then, to the next document, which is the letter you referred to, a letter to the mayor of Bosanski Novi, and which -- just check that. Yes. Thank you. It's there. You've just gone --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that one. That's not a letter to the mayor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Usher can you give it to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you put it on the ELMO, usher, please, one moment, are we safe with -- Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first page can go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first page, okay, I mean I have no problems with that but the second page may be problematic because of the person who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we look at the second paragraph of the first page, one might have some concern also. I don't know. It's up to Ms. Korner of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, there is no concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, there I wouldn't think so but I thank you for pointing at that, Mr. Ackerman, but I wouldn't think so either. But the second page, yes, but I leave it in the hands of Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much Your Honour, I was aware of that but the first page is all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is addressed to the mayor of Bosanski Novi, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And dated the 20th of June, from UNHCR, and you were obviously provided with a copy. Dear Mr. Pasic, I would like to thank you for your visit together with Mr. Rade to Topusko on the 28th of May, 1992, meeting with civil affairs coordinator Mr. Charles Kirudja and myself. I wish to assure you that since the meeting we have tried to follow the situation closely and have strong concerns for the welfare of the large number of Muslims in your community. On June the 13th, 1992, the special envoy of the high commissioner for refugees, Mr. J.M. Mendiluce sent a representative, Mr. Concolato and myself to the area. And on the 13th -- on June the 13th, 1992, we had an opportunity to review the situation with Mayor Borojevic in Dvor. Unfortunately, it was not possible for us to come across to meet with you and see the situation. As you will recall at our meeting, you named Mr. Barjaktarevic and Mr. Hamzagigic as spokespersons for the group and understood to arrange a meeting to talk with them. By this letter, I would like to inquire into what arrangements you have made for the meeting. If possible, we would also be interested in meeting with Mr. Izet Muhamedagic and a representative from local Red Cross/crescent or Merhamet. I would appreciate if you could contact the two individuals on our behalf and request them to suggest a meeting date. We suggest the venue of the meeting be Dvor. I would also like to stress the importance that UNHCR as an international humanitarian organisation places on the protection of these people in their home region so that their fundamental human rights are respected and to avoid the creation of a new flow of refugees. I am sure you realise your responsibility as the head of local government in that respect. With respect to the proposed mass transfer of population, I am sure that I do not need to remind you that since the Second World War, the forced, mass transfer of population on purely ethnic or racial basis has been declared a crime against humanity in international law. You are probably also aware that on November the 26th to the 27th, 1991, the parties to the conflict in the former Yugoslavia agreed at a conference convened at the initiative of the International Committee of the Red Cross to apply the provisions of international humanitarian law in the present conflict. I trust that you will agree with me on the importance of your responsibility in seeing to it that these international obligations are respected within your jurisdiction. Please allow me to include with this letter a copy of a folder on the work of UNHCR. At our meeting we also discussed the possibilities for international assistance for displaced persons in your municipality and I therefore also enclose a questionnaire to assess the needs for assistance regarding displaced persons in your municipality. And I look forward to hearing from you. Now, this letter, did you see it before it was written or -- I mean in other words, did you discuss it with the gentleman from UNHCR before it was written or were you just supplied with a copy afterwards?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the letter itself refers to in the very first paragraph, it refers to my -- to the meetings with me. Recall the earlier letter that this letter was intended to place beyond doubt with regard to the representatives of Bosanski Novi that sought a meeting with me about our position on the matter. So this letter was drafted at my request and my participation with the UNHCR gentlemen to make sure that it comes out clear. I didn't feel that my responsibility as the head civilian head of the mission, this matter technically was really not under my responsibility as a peacekeeping matter. Since the issue we are raising fell squarely under the international obligations of which UNHCR is a custodian. So we agreed, and that it will be drafted together but the signed -- signatory of that letter would probably be the UNHCR person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The paragraph in respect of the mass transfer being a breach or crime against humanity, was that something with which you agreed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, going back to the responsibility, I had them research that and have them phrase it the way UNHCR would -- will be consistent with what they knew about the UNHCR and ICRC so I let them research that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again, you said they did the research. Whether or not it's -- you're right, it is a legal matter but?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But as far as you were concerned, was this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour this is a matter for the Court, not a matter for this witness. It's up to you to decide whether that's a violation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are partly right but not completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. You're partly right, but not completely. In fact, I was going to invite you to put the question in some different manner because you were not getting there any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact I appreciated the point Mr. Ackerman has just made which is why I changed the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, from what you had seen and the conversations you had had, was this, as it is stated, a mass transfer of population on ethnic grounds? Leave aside whether it's a crime or not.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely the point I wanted clear because yesterday I made allusion to despite repeated oral explanation that this is not a -- the right thing for you to do, I mentioned yesterday that having heard me, they wanted me to tell them who my boss was so they can take up this matter higher. So I wanted this made clear to them that this is a mass transfer, 5.000 is no small number of people, and it isn't right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you and the gentleman who wrote the letter consulted over it. The purpose of saying this in the letter was what?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to make sure that he understood that this will not go well with the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes, thank you. If we move to the next document that's in the bundle that you sent, this I think we see next the original message that came from DanBat, the Danish Battalion. I really think we must try and -- dated the 20th of June, directed for your attention, subject refugees, 1, at whatever I think this must be on the 20th at 1020?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No it's time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Time.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 2000 hours, contacted nine refugees in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: B company in Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In Dubica, they are of something Serbian-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mixed, thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Origin and want either UN protection or help to get through to Zagreb. Then there is a problem about the kidney patients in Dvor having difficulty in getting their medicine, previously this has been transported by air from Belgrade to Banja Luka and Dvor claims that the -- this air space is now controlled by Croatian forces, DanBat doubts this, and then a further time, and this is the message you referred to, scouts from E company observed 15 people being gathered at the stadium in Bosanski Novi, the 15 people were guarded by people in camouflage uniforms and people surrounding the stadium waved white flags and flashed SOS in order to attract the attention of the DanBat scouts. DanBat has informed, I think this is, the city of Dvor that this matter will be reported and that DanBat is concerned for the fate of the people in the stadium. Then the next document should be, and perhaps the usher could give it to me, just find it --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Covering page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I think, Mr. Resch kindly suggests it's easier if his copy goes because the copy for the exhibit has been copied on both sides which makes it more difficult to find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay with me, Ms. Korner. The only thing is second page again, the very end is the name of the person to whom --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the ICRC person that I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- no the -- I think the only concern we need have is for the people working for UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this, Mr. Kirudja, was written by Mr. Raffone, I think, again, but released on your authority; is that correct, it's a letter of the 20th of June?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Addressed -- well, we'll see it was in fact addressed to the ICRC in Zagreb but copied to UNHCR and to the civil affairs headquarters in Zagreb. This letter describes a meeting in Velika Kladusa with the representative of the 850 displaced persons from Sanski Most. I think this is the first reference we've seen to Sanski Most. Was this the first time that you had any dealings with problems in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the first time we get a hint on that. This is the first time the people themselves are -- if you recall the previous meeting of 27th May, when Mr. Pasic came to my office, we already had been telegraphed the problems in Sanski Most, Prijedor and other places.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. The secretary of the Red Cross of Velika Kladusa, Mr. Muhamedagic, convened a meeting with the representative of the 850 displaced persons arrived from Sanski Most on the 12th of June, and the meeting took place on the 19th of June, 1992, at the local Red Cross headquarters. The civil affairs officer from Sector North and the chief of the station of UN CIVPOL of Slunj were invited to attend -- assist. The representative of the group of displaced persons from Sanski Most asked to keep his name anonymous. The report which follows is solely based on his statements. The witness of this forced evacuation was kept arrested in the sports hall of Sanski Most during 16 days, together with his son. Persons between 16 and 60 years were kept in this place. He declared that every day the persons kept in this place counted themselves to be sure that no one was missing. He counted some 250 persons missing since he arrived. They were asked to go out, he said, and never came back. The guards to this place were under the direction of a man who is the commander of the Serbian crisis committee of Banja Luka, Mr. Davidovic. In those days, the local radio reported that 230 extremist Green Berets were imprisoned in the concentration camp in Banja Luka. He added. The camp is called Manjaca and is some 30 kilometres out of Banja Luka. In this camp there are only dangerous war prisoners, [in inverted commas, extremists], some doctors and members of the SDA, he explained. Pausing for a moment, Mr. Kirudja, had you heard of Manjaca before this occasion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the beginning of the shape of information that later became subject of a very controversial memo that we put out. This is the beginning of our getting to see in detail and it became even more so as we interviewed all of these people one by one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the 11th of June, 1992, some 1.000 persons arrived in the sports hall. The same day, the authorities [Mr. Davidovic guards] organised ten buses and under the threat of heavy guns forced some of the people who were kept into the sports hall to go into the buses. He counted some 800 persons. The buses travelled up to Bosanska Krupa. In this place, again under the threat of heavy guns, all the persons were forced to get out of the buses and stand in line. All of us had to pass a bridge walking between the mines. On the other side, there were Green Berets and some local authorities waiting for us. Some transportation was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. arranged for us. On the 12th of June, the group arrived in Velika Kladusa. The local Red Cross helped the group and the Red Cross counted 850 persons, women, children and men above 60 years. All of them are Muslims. The man explained that all the group is presently hosted in local families but there is no food for them because there is not even -- there is not food even for the local population. The representative of the 850 persons from Sanski Most said that all of them would very much like to have the possibility to go back to their houses. Alternatively, he asked about the possibility of being evacuated from Velika Kladusa to Croatia. He explained that a good number of them owned houses in Croatia or have relatives there. And the secretary of the Red Cross said that unconfirmed news announced some three -- some new 3.000 displaced persons to arrive in Velika Kladusa from Bihac. By this stage, how were you and your fellow relief organisations regarding this flow of refugees that appeared to be arriving?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forgot to mention there was still another concern in trying to get this information as in dire terms that appear here. Earlier yesterday, I also mentioned that UNHCR and ICRC had taken a decision in their headquarters to pull out completely out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, following the killings of one of the ICRC delegations earlier, around May. You may recall that point that I made earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And at this moment, as you can see, I am addressing ICRC in this memo, that -- and especially a gentleman by the name shown there [as said]. I had met him a couple of times and we had begun to make head way in understanding that ICRC had to return into this area. We wanted them to make a reversal of their decision to pull out, as well as UNHCR. So there again in recognition of the fact that this is a matter far beyond UNPROFOR mission but it is coming inside. Velika Kladusa is on the border. It's not very far. It's about 20 minutes drive from Topusko so we knew this was going to be a major problem for us if we don't get other UN agencies involved in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 15, line 21, I think he said a name but has come out with the word "shown there," instead of that name, either that are I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no he did mention a name and it was, to me it sounded something like that. 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 21, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Line 21.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, just tell us the name, Mr. Kirudja, again, who you were trying to address, Mr. Schomburg or something like that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who I was what?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said you were trying to get the attention of Mr. --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, in this memo that it in front there is Philippe Noel, you can see the Philippe Noel, whom I had met a couple of times on the ground and he had shown us a good understanding and we were working with him, together the ICRC to understand the extent of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think the rest of the correspondence which you attached we have already been through because it goes back to the beginning of June. The purpose of sending all of this correspondence to headquarters was what?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I mentioned also yesterday, I had great difficulties with my headquarters, understanding or even accepting that what we were doing was not beyond the mandate or we were crossing the other border so first we had to make sure that this was a daily occurrence, this is a situation that we could not look the other way. These people coming from this areas that we mentioned, the only place of refuge they could find was where the UN flag was, and we were sitting below that UN flag. And secondly, being known Muslims, the Bosnian enclave of Bihac, first also was a less hostile area for them to gather first when they want to find refuge beyond, but across the border from that enclave of Bihac pocket it was a Serb-controlled area and that's where the UN was deployed, and they were themselves, the Serbs in that area where the UN was involved, as my meetings in Dvor show, they were also involved in this matter themselves. Therefore, we were consequently involved. And therefore, we needed the assistance of the two agencies, UNHCR and ICRC best suited to deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then move on to as you describe it the report that you sent on the 4th of July, which I think caused, as you say, something of a furore, that is please Exhibit P1671. Dated the 3rd of July, a memorandum headed "Humanitarian aid" and if we just turn over the page, it's addressed to a Ms. Y. Auger.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Auger.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Auger. DDCA Belgrade. And a Mr. -- and copied to Mr. Magnusson. And Ms. Auger was what?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was Mr. Cedric's immediate deputy in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, that's Mr. Magnusson?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Auger. Magnusson was another aide but he didn't have the title. Ms. Auger outranked him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Subject, humanitarian aid, I refer to your subject memo of 1st of July, 1992. The football field in Bosanski Novi is clearly visible from the town of Dvor in the UNPA. Further to our many previous reports on this, let me clarify that our sense of frustration is not, as stated in Mr. Magnusson's subject memo to the FC?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Force commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Force commander.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nambiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Our inability to investigate this matter. Can we pause there for a moment? So Mr. Magnusson had sent a memo to General Nambiar, had he?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be -- try again. At this moment, I'm almost seething with anger about this matter. I have to say that. I'm seething with anger. I have sent numerous messages to this headquarters in Zagreb, and now I'm told that you are unable to investigate this matter. We were being misread by Magnusson and I intended to put him on notice that it is not an inability to investigate this matter. Had I been even more blunt, I would have -- or daring I would have said it's because nobody is paying attention to what we are sending to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is really what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say you're seething with anger, that was then in July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I still -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I believe you have received a stream of reports not only of Bosanski Novi but also for other flash points along the border with BH. Bihac, Cazin, Velika Kladusa and Bosanska Dubica. In these reports we highlighted the following points: We believe the football field detainees are only a tip of the iceberg involving the concerted action of local Serbian authorities in BH trying to establish a Serbian Republic of BH, free of Muslims. In that process, the mayors, the militia and the TDF of Bosanski Novi acting in unison with their counterparts not only in the UNPA, Dvor and Kostajnica, but also with Bosanska Dubica, Banja Luka, Prijedor, Sanski Most and Kljuc. Now, in this part of the letter, you said acting not only with Dvor but with Dubica, Banja Luka, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc. You've already explained to us that you've been given reports from Prijedor and Sanski Most and I think Kljuc. What about Banja Luka? How did that come into it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- you will recall there was a telephone call received by Mr. Paolo Raffone where Mr. Kupresanin had also alluded to the same towns and warning from his own count 15.000 people had left the area of Banja Luka and warning that 15.000 more would follow, and then saying to us, "Please, the international organisation, we need the assistance of the humanitarian agencies in this crisis."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The Serbs appear to be engaged in a determined process of forcefully disarming Muslims where they are clearly a small encircled minority, such as in Bosanski Novi or besieging their city totally, such as in Bihac. Apparently, the football field is their holding ground where Muslim groups are detained while their houses are being, in inverted commas searched, the men isolated and transported to concentration camps. The UNHCR representative and civil affairs have pieced together reports from Muslims who recently have taken refuge under UNPROFOR protection in Dvor and Kostajnica. There are reported concentration camps at the following locations: Keraterm located at a railroad station in Prijedor en route to Banja Luka, 100 to 200 Muslims believed to be here under extremely bad conditions. Trnopolje: Also located at a railroad station in Prijedor, direction Banja Luka; a refugee camp for women, children and old men. Omarska: Located in a purely Serbian village, reportedly a camp for Muslim men and local Muslim authorities prior to Serbian takeover of control, particularly in Prijedor. Manjaca: Outside Banja Luka, a large camp reportedly including Croatian soldiers taken prisoner in the fighting in Kostajnica. The treatment of Muslims and other minorities in the camps is reportedly atrocious with regular beatings, deprivation of food and water, poor shelter, et cetera. Today in a meeting with ICRC and UNHCR, the above subject of humanitarian aid was discussed. The ICRC informed us that they will be deployed in BH and took the information we had on the subject. They also informed us that the ICRC will deploy a delegate or two specifically in Sector North to be located either in Vojnic or Glina. This in our view is a very positive step which we had recommended to the ICRC as a matter of urgency. Our frustration arises from our inability to do anything other than write reports and stand by. Since UNPROFOR has no operational responsibilities across the border. In recent days, the situation has deteriorated and has now begun to spill over to the UNPA. We have seen a mounting number of desperate people who have crossed over to seek refuge and protection from UNPROFOR. Yesterday, one Mustafa Ogorinac swam across the River Una at 5.00 in the morning from a camp in Bosanska Dubica. He is now under UNPROFOR protection along with two other persons. He shows signs of physical abuse and punishment. In a separate communication dated the 30th of June, I appealed to the special envoy of the UNHCR for one temporary measure to help to cope with the situation while waiting for the ICRC and UNHCR to resume their operations in BH. We have requested a minibus with driver to help in transporting the escapees to safety, since UN vehicles are not to be used for humanitarian purposes. Any assistance you can lend on the acquisition of the 16 to 20 seat minibus and driver is most appreciated. Regards. Now, the camps that you mentioned, these were camps that you had heard about, had you, from the refugees, displaced persons? We will just wait, I think, then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour while we are waiting I just sort of have a time concern that I want to -- Ms. Korner has now read in their entirety two of these letters this morning. I know that Your Honours are capable of reading. The questions seem to go to one small part of the letters and we just seem to be using up a lot of time reading documents that we can all read, and if that's okay with Your Honours, then it's okay with me. It just seems to me from a time standpoint it's wasteful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I propose to go on in the way I have because I think it's important first of all because people are watching and it's no good just taking up parts like that and second because I think it's important that we go through these. I've said I'll finish today and I will. That gives Mr. Ackerman two clear days to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Go ahead for the time being and then we see how it develops but try to restrict yourself because I'm pretty sure that in every letter there may be paragraphs that are -- I know that you have skipped some in other documents but -- any way, I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I'm sorry, now that the banging has stopped, Mr. Kirudja, the camps that you mention here, that's information you got from the refugees or displaced persons, is it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This again back in context, we have seen these number of refugees, beginning with the one that had gathered in Velika Kladusa. Those who had crossed, we had all of -- a lot of them in a hotel in Vojnic. My colleagues spent sleepless nights with them one by one and pieced together the information that they summarised in this memo, but it was also something else. It's very condensed, as you can see, because I'm talking about my headquarters, talking about not telling them, talking about we are unable to investigate. So I wanted it concise and clear: This is what we are facing. This is what the consequences are. And we don't have a choice about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did anybody, when you sent this memorandum, to your knowledge, do anything about this?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. It was never -- I wasn't even sure anybody else cared about it, until General Nambiar called me later on, towards -- one or two days later. And he called me because he was concerned about the language "concentration camp." General Nambiar was a very careful man. I respect him a lot and I worked with him very well. So he called me and said, "Why are you sure it's a concentration camp?" And I said to him, come to think of it, we just translated -- we just wrote down what the interpreter said the people called them, the people talking to us, and the interpreter talking to us said we have a concentration camp in these places. Now, recall, these are people in the former Yugoslavia, expected to know the meaning of the word "concentration camp." Second World War was something that most of them were familiar with. So I said to the general, okay, what would you call it, then, if I wouldn't -- if the term is -- could they then be detention camps? That was the purpose for him calling me just to be sure that our language was not necessarily alarmist. The next thing I knew is that there is headquarters, about a month or so, concerned when this memo became a major brouhaha, leaked out by some places at headquarters in New York. It was on radio, it was on television, and somebody at the head of the DPKO came to see me in Sector North and they wanted to know who leaked the memo. That's all they were concerned, who leaked the memo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hear at any stage about the killings that had taken place in a place called Room 3 in Keraterm at the end of July?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were also careful not to go into greater detail about this because we were in Sector North. This was in Bosnia, no mandate of the UN. So we restricted the details that we were involved in, just to serve notice that these people are here in Sector North or across the border coming from these places.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in respect of Omarska, did you become aware, at the beginning of August, of the news bulletins that were obtained by an English television crew, Penny Marshall, at any stage?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one moment, I had 30 -- 30 or plus, I stopped counting, journalists in my office on Sector North when this memo was out and television crews.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Just can you remember when it was leaked, when it came out, roughly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I am in Sector North, where very rarely had I any communication outside. As soon as I sent my memos under restricted thing I wouldn't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can we move then, please, to the next memorandum that you wrote, or rather Mr. Raffone wrote, P1672? This is dated the 8th of July, subject, arriving refugees from Bosanski Novi, on the 7th of July, 1992, a group of 18 persons arrived in Sector North from Bosanski Novi asking for protection and assistance to cross the CFL?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Towards Zagreb or other foreign countries. The civil affairs officer interviewed the group and arranged for the crossing on the 8th of July. Was that you or Mr. Raffone there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Mr. Raffone, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The following information is based solely on the statements of these persons who have asked for anonymity for security reasons. In Bosanski Novi the Muslim ethnic group, 28 per cent, continue to suffer persecution, deportation and intimidation from Serbian armed groups. The beginning of this crisis is traced back to the end of April, 1992. The persons interviewed reported that all Muslims living in the town and in the neighbouring villages are ready to leave the area towards Croatia or other destinations in Europe. Previously, we reported that the stadium of Bosanski Novi is one of the places where hundreds of persons have been held for screening following which they are expelled from the area towards unknown destinations. Reportedly, all Muslims are forced to sign papers asking them to voluntarily leave under the following conditions: Leave behind all personal property, including cars, personal effects, et cetera; swear that they were permanently leaving the area and that they will never go back to their houses. Following compliance with these conditions, they are issued a declaration from the local TDF commander and the militia or the mayor, allowing them to leave their opstina of residence. They are generally forced to leave in the direction of Dvor. It is reported the local authorities in Dvor do not seem surprised at the arrival of the forcefully removed persons. They even show a cooperative effort to facilitate their way towards Croatian-controlled territories. A calculated strategy to cleanse the area of Muslims appears to have intensified, beginning in May of 1992. House burnings, deportations, summary executions, shooting in the houses, et cetera, are part of the present situation in the towns and villages along the north side of the BH border. Bosanski Novi, Kostajnica, Dubica. Reportedly the militia does not seem to intervene. Some mayors and other Serbs working in the opstinas have also been reported as trying to help the Muslims to leave their house safely. In Bosanski Novi the military police has reported to have its HQ in the Hotel Una. There are reports of brutal torture in the hotel. The persons interviewed believe that the political leaders know what is happening. Some of them attest allegations that some high level politicians in the SDS party are known to have given orders for actions against Muslims. Some of the refugees tell of a retaliatory policy of one Serbian killed in the front line, one Muslim man will be killed. All the men interviewed had been held for some days in the stadium of Bosanski Novi before being expelled. They report that every day some 30 new detainees arrived in the stadium. When the stadium is full, the guards take some of them away to unknown destinations. Some witnesses report that in the first 15 days of May, that some 200 persons taken out of the stadium were shot dead nearby. Based on these interviews, the persons estimated that some 5.000 persons may try to cross the bridge between Novi and Dvor in the coming days. This letter signed by him to the -- your headquarters but copied to all the other organisations. As far as you and your staff were concerned, from what you were seeing, could all these matters that had happened in different municipalities have been isolated, spontaneous incidents?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. By this time, no. We had of course come to the conclusion that this is, as you put it, not an isolated incident, the people are coming from one end of the border with Bosnia, from Bosanska Dubica, which was closest to the edge of our sector all the way down to Bihac and in between, and there were different opstinas that this area comprised. It was clear, to conclude, this could not have been an isolated matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The persons, according to Mr. Raffone interviewed believe that the political leaders know what is happening. Had you from your own observations or conversations, any view on that matter?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must also draw your attention that this letter comes at the wake of -- after the meeting with Pasic himself. So as I -- as Mr. Raffone was summarising what was hearing from his direct interviews with the people, the part it was corroborating what Mr. Pasic and his colleagues were asking me directly to do. So there was no new information to me in that regard. What it did is serve notice that it is coming from different angles that is the purpose for me releasing this memo it's coming from different place but the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So sorry, Mr. Kirudja, the question was: They were saying Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. political leaders knew what was happening. Was that your view as well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my view that the mayors and the police chiefs, if that's what you meant, in each opstina, knew about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could we then move, please, now, to the following day -- sorry, it's Exhibit 1673, the 12th of July. And I think we just put the front page up because this is another UNHCR letter. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Ms. Korner, I see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, can we take that off, Your Honour, thank you very much. It's the same gentleman from UNHCR that we'd seen the earlier correspondence from.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is this again something that before it was sent was discussed with you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dated the 12th of July. This -- I can summarise quite a lot of this. He received a message on the 7th of July that there were 79 refugees outside the police station in Dvor. When he got there on the 8th of July, and had briefings with DanCon, it turned out that the persons had left the station before and returned to Bosanski Novi, and so then a meeting was called with the deputy mayor, the chief of the militia, but in fact they were unable to attend at shot notice. During the duration of the three hour meeting new Muslims had arrived at the CIVPOL station and he said he was able to interview two family representatives who then returned to Bosanski Novi. Then the situation, he deals with. The background can be found in some acts of the public authorities in the days before. On the 6th of July, 1992, the crisis committee of Bosanski Novi addressed a letter to civil affairs, which was given to me by CIVPOL. According to the letter, the crisis committee informed that 1233 persons had applied to authorities for permission to leave and the community would help provide transport for those Muslims who did not have their own means of transportation. And a copy of the document with translation is appended and we will have a look at that in a moment. 7th of July meeting between the mayor, advice mayor and chairman of the assembly of Dvor and other representatives of the humanitarian organisations, and again this refers to what's in your memorandum about what people had to do before they could leave. The Bosanski Novi informed that they processed applications from 1300 families who all fulfilled the criteria. They estimate that this amounts to a total of some 3.000 to 5.000 persons different from the 5.000 Muslims in convoy reported on by the end of May, 1992, who by and large had escaped, been sent away by other routes which are no longer open due to the fighting. And then at the beginning of the meeting, on the 8th of July, the Dvor representatives gave us a copy of the order from the Crisis Staff of the Dvor municipality in regard to the Novi situation. And effectively saying they weren't going to allow passage unless it was by UNPROFOR. At the meeting the deputy mayor stressed that his community did not want to do anything without UNPROFOR. Paragraph 11. The chief of police said that the refugee cases started some eight to ten days ago but after the large increase, it became a problem, how many people have already exchanged their houses with Serbs from Croatia. The deputy mayor did not want to second guess the reason why people wanted to leave but later volunteered his own opinion. Some had been disappointed in the politics of Izetbegovic, further after the fighting in the Cazin and Kladusa region and with the return of wounded and killed Serbs, Muslims in the area were getting afraid of revenge from relatives. As the discussions got more frank, they did not contest that it was very questionable whether the request to leave had been signed voluntarily. When I asked them to confirm that the mayors of Bosanski Novi and Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- stating that Muslims and Serbs could no longer live together they said it was not the mayor but the chief of the crisis committee in Banja Luka, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, I'm asked to draw your attention to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm speeding up, trying to help Mr. Ackerman out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then the paragraph -- the letter goes on that try to separate the issues of humanitarian assistance, and then we see in paragraph 14 that on the 8th of July, UNHCR, OSCE, as well as the Croatian authorities were briefed in Zagreb on the matter by the civil affairs coordinator, Mr. Kirudja. So Mr. Kirudja, at the time of this meeting, on the 8th of July, you were actually in Zagreb, were you, briefing the authorities there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On July?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 8th of July, 1992, if you just check your --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I don't think we need trouble actually with the end of this document but can I go back do that paragraph about which mentions Mr. Brdjanin? Was that a name you had heard at all by July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about him other than in this document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, thank you. Then if we could move through what happened next, can we go please to document 1675? -- 4, I'm sorry, first, sorry. A memo again from Mr. Raffone dated the 13th of July, 5.000 Muslim refugees from Bosanski Novi, following our phone call earlier today, please find attached a self-explanatory note from UNHCR concerning the possible arrival of some 5.000 persons displaced refugees from Bosanski Novi to UNPA north. And if we look at the accompanying document, rather, not terribly clear, but it talks about a meeting on the 11th of July between UNHCR and the mayors and chiefs of police and Bosanski Novi. The main issue the local authorities on both sides trying to get support and approval from UNHCR and UNPROFOR to arrange the transit of 3500 to 5.000 Muslims from BH. Paragraph 2: UNHCR and UNPROFOR stated clearly that participating in displacement or movement of population could never be expected, that no guarantee of safety could be provided through transit, et cetera. And then 3, after the meeting, UNHCR crossed into Bosanski Novi and met representatives of the Muslim population wanting and preparing to leave. Despite all explanations their attitude remained the same, i.e. that their only possibility is to leave Bosnian Krajina for destinations in Croatia, Slovenia and Western Europe. And then it deals -- and then at the bottom, that apparently on the 11th of July, reportedly a number of buses with Serbs from north and north-eastern parts of Bihac entered the UNPA. Some of these arrivals had been confirmed and concerns are that we are facing another population movement where Croatian property and houses and UNPA north will be taken into use by Serbian population and local informers even mentioned volunteers from Belgrade in this context. I think you told us earlier, Mr. Kirudja, but you yourself never did cross the border into Bosanski Novi, did you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very careful not to do that. I was already being accused of extending UNPA concerns into Bosnia where we have no mandate so I was very careful not to cross it but I sent somebody else to cross it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Can we look, please, at P1675? A short memorandum for the same date, talking about the 20 busloads of refugees from Bosanski Novi crossing the border. Today an advance group of people from Bosanski Novi arrived at the gate of DanCon and announced that on Wednesday, the 15th of July, at 12 noon, 20 bus loads of refugees will arrive in Dvor. And they have been told that UNPROFOR won't be able to assist, the government of Croatia has given instructions to its border police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please read that slower and louder?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then if we move, all of this being the buildup to what actually happened, these two -- one Exhibit P1676. Again, this is from Mr. Raffone, I think, and --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the one I have, 21 July?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just see what you've got there? Sorry, the -- oh, sorry. Just a moment. Sorry, Your Honour, it's my fault. It's actually in a different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it 1676 or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no the one I was looking at isn't, it was document 31 of Mr. Kirudja's documents so it doesn't make much difference I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document as you say signed by you on the 21st of July, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And sorry, I just want to -- all right. Let's deal with that and I'm going to ask for a break because my numbering seems to have gone somewhat -- dated the 21st of July, subject refugees. We have received a copy of Andreev's message of -- is that 1409, July 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14 of July, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Before we go on, Mr. Andreev being whom?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Andreev was my counterpart based in Knin Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then he says, and he'd sent a message, had he, about refugees from Bihac clearly, judging by the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would advise that this should be considered as different from the 4.000 refugees expected to transit through Sector North in the next two days from Bosanski Novi. The UNHCR has obtained the consent of the Croatian government to allow passage of the 4.000, copy of a self explanatory letter from Prime Minister Greguric is attached and then it talks about the logistics of transit involving some 45 buses and 200 cars from Bosanski Novi to Karlovac and then the logistics and then repeating, the 10.000 refugees mentioned by Andreev are over and above the arrangements being made to transit through Sector North. I'd be grateful if Andreev could apprise the authorities in Knin of these developments. And then you enclosed the letter from the government of the Republic of Croatia. In fact addressed to Mr. Mendiluce, and appears as follows: Dear sir we received your letter describing the present situation of ethnic cleansing in Novi, as reported by your group of senior officers from UNHCR Zagreb. And then it does say that as a last solution, they will allow these people into the Republic of Croatia. Mr. Kirudja, had that -- had it been difficult to persuade the government of Croatia to take this?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, we regarded the letter as an anticlimax. We had, as you read earlier, worked strenuously to be sure that this number of people do not get moved, and we were at the same time in touch with the Croatian side, who sustained our position that we wouldn't allow such a movement to be undertaken. They held that line until somewhere within the time period last few days of that letter, for other consideration for which I wasn't privy they decided they will accept 4.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes, and really I think I can finish this off. Although I have -- I thought my numbering system had gone wrong, so I need to back here for a couple of things. But effectively, did this convoy pass through on the 23rd of July?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did but not in the numbers that were expected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: More or less?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: More. Instead of 4.000, over 9.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, could we just take the break five minutes early while I redo my numbering system?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will take a 25 minute break and resume soon after.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we may as well get the witness but I don't know where Mr. Ackerman is. Perhaps the usher can get the witness and perhaps somebody could tell us where Mr. Ackerman is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought we had lost you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The door was locked and I was standing in the hall and couldn't get in. It's not unusual. I'm defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While we wait for Mr. Kirudja to come in, I have missed out part of the document. That's what was worrying me. It's 1672, so if the Registrar could find that one again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I've had a complete telling off from the interpreters so I think I better put the ear phones on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I'm going to ask you, please, to have back P1672, because I did miss out some of the attachments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document enclosed the letter referred to from Mr. Pasic and a document and clearly, the authorities had done their own English translation of the original letter and we had a proper translation done which makes it slightly clearer. I hope Your Honours have got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We went through the first of these documents from Mr. Raffone but I think enclosed with it, Mr. Kirudja, were documents that had been sent and translated or part of it translated, by Mr. Pasic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we then look, please, and I'd like you to be given --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, it may be my own interpreters. I can't be sure whether it is Pasic. Usually my own interpreters at Sector North were able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to insult them but I think we had a slightly better interpretation done of it. I wonder if you could be given just for a moment, please, the new translation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it attached to here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How would I be able to tell the difference between the new one and the old one? Or do I not have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Ackerman. You were sent -- there is a translation done into English, it was with the original documents done either by Mr. Kirudja's interpreters or by the authorities in Bosanski Novi. We retranslated it and you've got that. You were given that sometime ago.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's no good shrugging, you've got it. If you don't have it, it's not our fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not disagreeing, Ms. Korner. I'm just suggesting that I don't have it here in front of me. I totally trust that you gave it to me at one point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We've got one more copy, again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This was a letter dated the 6th of July, from apparently Mr. Pasic. It was stamped and signed.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, I have a copy of the translation of my own memo in Serbian, and the one that you want to focus on isn't in this set. It's not in the set you just gave me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kirudja, there is always this problem about --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This is a translation of the stamped Serbian letter which there was already a translation of.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Still not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, for heaven's sake. No. It's no point giving Mr. Kirudja the Serbian translation. It's the English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The documents the usher brought to me just a moment ago as the English translation were all in Serbian, so I support that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour there is a new translation I'm not going to bother with this. Let's just look at the one they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Kirudja, if we look very -- and I think we can summarise it through your own translation, there was a letter dated the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In which they said that they wanted 1233 persons had applied to leave, given all the required statements, and then the statements -- statements of immovable property and asked for the meeting with the representatives. And then safeguarding the convoy will be provided by internal affairs. And then also attached, I think, was another document which in fact you didn't apparently get translated but we have and when we find them, Your Honour, I think you've got them, it was the municipal Crisis Staff -- I think perhaps the best thing is if you haven't got it there, Mr. Kirudja, can we put this on the ELMO and then we can all see.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just going to see it myself. Dated the 8th of July, and discussing -- it talks about how it discussed a memo from Bosanski Novi municipal Crisis Staff concerning the voluntary departure, and then if we look, if you can move the document up the ELMO slightly, please, the Dvor public security station is instructed not to issue individual passes, only for migrant convoys, UNPROFOR civilian police requested to contact the government of the Republic of Croatia and after that, they would issue passes for the convoy and finally, 3, instructed to step up controls at the crossing point to prevent the passage of Muslim and other ethnicities. I think you referred to that or it was referred to in one of the documents we already read. Okay. And then I think the final document was another which I missed out, 9th of July memorandum by yourself, dealing with the position of the government of Croatia over these refugees. So thank you, we can now get rid of that rather difficult document.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, did Your Honours have that translation? You did, right so I don't know what's happened to everybody else's.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Kirudja, I'm sorry, there was one, as I said, my note system fell at this point, I think on the 10th of July, you had a meeting with the mayor of Dvor and the deputy mayor of Bosanski Novi, which is recorded in your diary, if you could have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have that meeting marked in my notes here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, this is page 26 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This -- was this a meeting, can you recall that you had asked for or that they asked for?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My notes don't clarify that, and -- but since it was in Dvor, again this was within our mandate, my area of Sector North, routine meetings there would have been -- it wouldn't have made a great difference who asked for it because it is inside the sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think it was about the issue of refugees?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were they claiming that they had to look after 7500 refugees from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did they say, however, something about the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mayor at this time was repeating same things that we had heard before by Mayor Borojevic. By then, I believe by this time, Borojevic had resigned or been moved. Yet the language from the deputy mayor is indistinguishable from the previous mayor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did they talk about allowing the Muslim population to leave?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- they -- my notes here show that they still are talking about voluntary people leaving through the sector. Again, notwithstanding the prior meeting where in writing I made clear this is -- there is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. nothing voluntary about this, and they are also telling us, and I quote, "UNPROFOR and UNHCR do not seem to believe that these people are leaving voluntarily and are being forced to leave. When you understand the problem will be solved." In short what the mayor is saying, "As soon as you change your mind about it, the problem will be solved. It's not a problem for Serbs in Bosanski Novi and need not ask for UNHCR assistance." It's a bit of defiance going on here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you interpret what was being said in respect of what was going to happen if UNHCR didn't assist or UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We will solve the problem by ourselves, they said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you think that -- what did you understand that they were going to solve the problem by what means?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By now, I was clear that no matter what we said, there was a determination to proceed this way. The number of the refugees that you mentioned earlier, number of 7.500 Serb refugees who were expelled from Bosanski Novi it was repeated again by the deputy mayor, the voluntary situation is also repeated. It's like a broken record. They will repeat that no matter what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he say something else, though? This is the mayor.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this specific meeting, I'm not sure that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can lead because I think --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless you have something specific that you want me to recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think because I'm sure Mr. Ackerman would like me to bring it out, but did he in fact at some stage say to you, I am the mayor of all people and I will see to it that Muslims will not be expelled?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that I can see here but this is after I said that -- and he said, "I am the mayor of all people in Bosanski Novi and we will extend the protection to Muslims. They will not be expelled." That I have here in my notes. I was talking about some other idea that, like football field or anything. I don't know whether that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. First of all, did you accept that, that statement, that he wasn't going to see -- that he would see that Muslims weren't expelled?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wrote it down because I -- I knew these people I had worked with them many, many times. There was always a back stepping whenever I increased our resistance to the idea. So it was his way of saying to me we are not trying to harm these people even if you don't believe they are leaving voluntarily. That's all he was trying to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, let's go back to, because we had gone ahead to the 23rd of July, and the actual convoy itself, but before that, had you heard -- had you heard anything from Mr. Thornberry about your actions?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Thornberry telling you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This time it's a memo he sent to me clearly saying you should not -- you should desist from this involvement you have with these refugees coming from Bosanski Novi -- from across the border into Bosnia because, according to Mr. Thornberry, the Security Council mandate does not extend across the border, something of course I would think he was right about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can see from what happened that you nonetheless proceeded. What was your view that you morally, whatever the mandate was, should be doing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant in this time, if you pardon my earlier comment that I had been frustrated a couple of times by sending these reports and not having anything happen, all -- but the misinterpretation and I considered it a misinterpretation that we were being involved across Bosnia. The message we were sending was, the UN location here is attracting the attention of all these people in dire straits. These people are not looking at the Security Council mandate. They are looking at the flag of the UN and they can see it clear and they think of it as a place of refuge. And to approach it in that narrow manner was to miss the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's move on, please, to the 22nd of July, Exhibit P1677. And I think we can summarise this document that was sent by you because that actually dealt with the transit UNHCR having dealt with the logistics of that. Next, please, could we look at -- all right. Yes, you've dealt with the evacuation, I'm sorry, the evacuation -- the number of people coming from Bosanski Novi well exceeding the figures that you had expected. I want now to move to, please, August, and could you have a look, please, at a document that was numbered document 37? Now, this is a slightly different, I think, report from the earlier ones we have been looking at. Was this --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, my copy is in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, we can see that it's addressed to Mr. Thornberry from you and it says attached is a civil affairs sit-rep dated the 22nd of August, 1992. Was this a regular sort of weekly report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of -- yes. This complements specific reports you have put in front of me which we would put up because of the subject on the day the subject occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also, at the end of the week, I was requested to put together a situation report that kind of put together for that week what was happening and giving it a better context of understanding, connecting documents where need was. So it would be called a situation report for that week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I want you to go, please, in that report, to the third page which is headed, "The border with Bosnia." In paragraph 9, the border with BH continues to be a zone of conflict and a source of pressure from refugees wishing to transit the UNPA to elsewhere in Croatia and beyond. And then you set out the problems it's causing. And then coming to paragraph 12, you talk about the delegation that came on the 19th of August. Can I just ask you this, though? Before that, had you had any meetings with Mr. Mendiluce about the expected arrival of further displaced persons or refugees?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my recollection I had met a number of times with Mr. Mendiluce, first in connection with the first batch of refugees that crossed, the one I said were more like 9.000. And thereafter, because we had warned if you do this, it only -- it's going to be only round 1, and there will be more coming. So this paragraph, paragraph 12, is talking about the attempt to cause round 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then it reads on the 19th of August, UNHCR and civil affairs received at Topusko a delegation of nine representatives, Serbs and Muslims, of Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa and Prijedor, all from BH. Their intention was to convince the UN to change its policy and assist in the organisation of a convoy through Sector North to evacuate up to 11.000 mostly Muslims from Sanski Most, 8.000 from Prijedor, and 600 from Bosanska Krupa. A detailed list of 7.782 names of those ready to leave voluntarily was delivered. Were you given this list?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date of this sit-rep is 26 August.
