The meeting took place a day or two earlier, I believe the 19th of August, where again the authorities from these towns on their own showed up in my office, from these places, Sanski Most, Prijedor and others. Literally they showed up in the office. They give me an indication of the numbers that they expect to come out of Sanski Most, 11.000; Prijedor, 8.000; Bosanska Krupa, 600; and so forth. At the same time, they give me a printed list, computer-produced, in the old printer where one page is attached to the next. It was a long, detailed list with the names and certain other details that I forget because this list for some reason was lost somewhere. I have never seen it since the last time I was looking at it in my office. It was a detailed, typed list and then we counted the names on it after they left, and that's why we came with the precise number of 7.782 names on that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think you made a note in your diary of the persons or some of the persons who attended that meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, then, at your note and tell us who was there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is page 34 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, there was Mr. Vlado Vrkes, president of the SDS, Sanski Most. There was Dragan Majkic, representatives of the militia of Sanski Most. There was a Mr. Besim Islamcevic, the representative of Muslims and Croatians willing to leave Sanski Most. There was a Mr. Esad Hasanovic, representative of Muslim refugees from Bosanska Krupa, now in Sanski Most -- at that time was in Sanski Most. That is shown at the front of my meeting. I believe somewhere inside the meeting there may be other people that were taken note of by my colleague, the gentleman from UNHCR, because I may have stopped writing as soon as they started speaking so I can take note of what they are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I don't think you made a note, did you, of the names of the persons from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is my indication that I may have stopped taking their names and started taking down their speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you tell us, from your notes, please, then, what was said at this meeting? Flesh out what is in that short report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, it was a request for round 2, that we allow, in a similar manner that was done in July, that these people pass through Sector North in a similar manner. At this moment, they were not talking to me about voluntarily. At that moment, that issue was not being reprised again. I was given the precise estimated numbers that would come from different places, and I have just given you those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they also listened to UNHCR reiterate the position that this is not something we are going to allow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you -- I think you made a note first of all of what Mr. Islamcevic said.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He started by saying, and I quote, "I'm authorised to say that the convoy should be escorted by UNPROFOR." In short I took that as a cue from him, I'm asked to say these things to you. And they were, "I am authorised" and then he proceeds to say. We don't want to go from one part of Bosnia to another and we do not want war. Have guarantees from relatives where we want to go to and we want to say Serbian authorities are treating us fairly. We want guarantees that none of the people will be taken out of the convoy from start to Karlovac. Karlovac was the destination where they would have crossed to the Croatian-controlled side of the sector. All other routes are routes to the unknown so this is the only route Mr. Islamcevic wanted his people to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Vrkes say something?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He started by saying there are 25.000 Muslims in Sanski Most. We accepted their other numbers in Bosanska Krupa, he didn't name a number. Sanski Most is the only opstina taking care of all the three nationalities, as the language used to refer to Serbs, Croats and Muslims, they were referred to them collectively as other nationalities. And he went on to say there were 50 per cent Serbs, 50 per cent Muslims and Croats in Sanski Most. Historically Muslims were not included in -- in these regions. Basically that is the cryptic -- I mean summary of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about what people had to do who wanted to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I underscore when I write these things and I'm in -- I'm the person they came to see in the meeting, and I don't always write everything that is here so my notes should not be considered as complete in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report I write following those notes should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So do you have anything in your notes about Mr. Vrkes telling you what people had to do in order to leave?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not directly here on the notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us whether anything was said by the representative from Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He started by expressing disappointment with the relationship between us and UNHCR. For one month our application pending and nothing done, in short our again typical that we had already signalled our unwillingness to participate. So he was expressing displeasure with that. And he went on to give credit to quote government help that he -- they were getting from Sanski Most. And -- but he went on to talk about every day we were being forced to leave the houses we are in. He stressed we have guaranteed accommodation and jobs, 80 per cent, in Slovenia and other countries. And he give me a copy of a guarantees that he said they were being given. He made reference to winter coming, and the conditions worsening as winter set on. He was requesting assistance to get to the places where they wanted to go and their vehicles were all ready for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he was a Muslim, was he, the gentleman from Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosanska Krupa representative, yes, he was billed as a representative of Muslim and Croatian willing to leave Sanski Most, from the name one would assume he would be Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What about Prijedor? Did the representatives from Prijedor say anything?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- I only have one line note from him. We have 8.000 requests for exits. Not all of these 8.000 are Muslims because some of them are mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if we look, then, please, back to the report, at paragraph 12, I think we see that the UNHCR repeated its policy of non-participation in such convoys from Bosnia, and that at the end of the meeting, the delegation left feeling that the UN was an obstacle to what one of them called a humanitarian gesture by the Serbs to Muslims reached through a democratic process. Do you remember who said that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned, all of them were focused on that disappointment since it wasn't vague, we said so. We intended to not to participate, and we said so. So you could assume on one side both the Muslims representatives felt that disappointment themselves because they wanted to leave in these places that they expressed they wanted to go and we were not helping in their own eyes. Of course, on the Serb side, they felt disappointed because we told them, in the language we used this morning, this is not something that the UN or UNHCR can participate in, because of its enormity and because of its implications, you're taking people from their homes and making refugees out of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, if we just finish that report, I'd like you to look at some documents outside of the ones you've produced. There was in paragraph 13, there was a report dated the 12th of August, saying that 10.000 refugees were scheduled to cross, and that the UN participation in the convoy could not be considered as supporting the ethnic cleansing policy. Pausing there for a moment, at this stage were you using the terms, and we can see this report generally, that this was ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were -- ourselves -- not trying to characterise things at this moment one way or the other, because we kept our eyes on the essence of the issue, those refugees and making sure if we insist that they don't cross, you also want to be sure that you're not condemning them into a situation where there will be killings and all others. You wanted to achieve two things. You wanted to serve notice hopefully that we were hoping the Serbs who were clearly forcing this issue to rethink and protect them, and you heard that statement from the mayor, we are not harming them, because we wanted him to understand we are looking but we are not going to move them any way. Secondly, then we wanted their protection. So we wouldn't use terms like that, other people outside the sector did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then finishing off this, she had no information on the 300.000 Muslims reported to be cut off in the city of Bihac. And everything we have heard or know from UNHCR is contrary to that press release. Most importantly, both the UNHCR and UNPROFOR representatives on the ground could find ourselves confronting local officials should they get a hold of that press release. And being told that we are acting contrary to official New York policy. It is not too long ago when local officials got hold of a story about a suppressed report of the Secretary-General which they used to advantage. There was no such suppressed report as we were later advised. And then, the last paragraph deals with the medical evacuations and the rest of the report, I think, with matters unconnected with this case.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, that report on -- is a reference to the document we saw this morning about concentration camps and what I mentioned earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours that one -- this document hasn't been exhibited yet so may it be made P1648?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what was given to us as document 37?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, before we go on to your next situation report, I want to you look, please, at some of the documents that were written by the Serbs themselves in relation to this issue, see how this accords with what you've been telling us. Could you have a look, please, first of all, at P709? This is a document that comes from the Sanski Most municipality, the executive committee, dated the 30th of July, and in item number 1, it states this at the third paragraph: There are currently about question mark 18.000 Muslims and Croats in the Sanski Most municipality area, and in order to avoid danger to the Serbian people, it is necessary to organise their voluntary resettlement. Now, that talks about, in July of 1992, and your meeting was on the 19th of August, some 18.000 Muslims and Croats. How does that figure marry up with what you were being told, can you say?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's recognisable in two aspects, that there were Muslims and Croats and they were in Sanski Most, and that there is an organisation of voluntary resettlement. That is what we were being told. And later on we didn't of course agree that it was voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did any of these representatives that you were talking to, particularly Mr. Vrkes or Mr. Vrunicic say to you that these people were a potential danger to the Serbs, that is the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims themselves were extremely cautious to -- when they were in front of us to give credit to their Serb colleagues that they are treating us well. But that's in our presence. It's not the same when we were interviewing the refugees coming from there. The opposite is being said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So but at that meeting, neither Mr. Vrunicic nor Mr. Vrkes, said to you we want them out because they are a danger or a potential danger?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now could you have a look please at another document from Sanski Most, P716? Now this one is dated the 17th of August so two days before the meeting, and it's addressed to the CSB in Banja Luka, for the chief, and signed by this gentleman who attended your meeting, Mr. Vrunicic, stating that at the beginning of August, the civilian and military organs of Sanski Most municipality adopted a decision and launched an initiative whereby citizens of Muslim or Croatian ethnicity can submit to the administrative organ of the municipal assembly a written request and a declaration of loyalty requesting that they be allowed to stay in the territory. A special municipal committee deals with these requests. And the SJB was given the task of issuing these permits. Since this concerned a document that is not prescribed by the law on the interior we ask to you give us instructions on how to proceed further with the issue of these permits. We should point out that this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. does not concern any new registration of residents and so on and so forth. Now, was there any discussion at that meeting between you and the representatives of Sanski Most about people who wanted to stay, giving a declaration of loyalty?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This matter had -- didn't come up at that meeting. It was only in the prior meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Again, I think I've asked you this but was there anything said by either of these gentlemen about the people who wanted to leave voluntarily, what they had to do?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was alluded to by the Muslim side of the representation that they had already received the necessary permits from the local Serbs and they said that with an air of gratefulness that we were -- we are ready to leave and it's us who -- us meaning UNPROFOR -- who are standing in the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You can put that document away. Now could you have a look please at parts of a very lengthy document, Exhibit P717? Now, this document was a lengthy report produced sometime after the 14th of August, dealing with a number of municipalities, the first being Prijedor, and I'd like you to find, please, it's on the 4th page, resettlement of citizens from the municipality of Prijedor. This is in fact was the commission who produced this report. About -- according to this, to the SJB Prijedor, about 4.000 to 5.000 persons, mainly of Muslim ethnicity left the municipality before the armed conflict. The armed conflict began at the end of May, Mr. Kirudja. Were you receiving refugees from Prijedor before the end of May?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure that we did or didn't. What I have reported to is the constant stream of different refugees, so I can't answer directly to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then the second paragraph, from the beginning of the armed conflict, in the municipality of Prijedor, until the 16th of August, 1992, according to data that had been insufficiently checked out, about 20.000 citizens left the municipality, mainly of Muslim and Croatian but also of Serbian ethnicity. Of all ages and groups. And then on the 16th of August, Prijedor SJB received and made positive rulings on 13.180 applications to unregister the legal places of residence. Mainly from citizens of Muslim nationality who expressed the desire to depart for the Republic of Slovenia or other countries of Western Europe. This group has not left the municipality but has just completed the unregistering of residences and is now with the help of religious and humanitarian organisations looking for a way of resettling in the desired direction. Prijedor SJB has no data about what these people have done with their immovable assets or what they have done or will do with their movable assets. Now, does that accord, this paragraph, three days before your meeting, with what you were being told by the Prijedor representatives at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does only indirectly in the sense that they informed us of 8.000, which is a subset of the number given in that paragraph. It would be a problem if the number they told us was bigger than that number but since it's less I assume it's a subset of that number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They however, this expression, desire to depart for the Republic of Slovenia or other countries of Western Europe, I think that was something that was mentioned in your record of the meeting, was it not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is constant. It was in that meeting. It was in the meeting before and it is a constant reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then we can go on in the report, we come to Sanski Most at page 7, page 6 is the reception centres. The sports hall I think was what was mentioned in that report that we saw as one of the so-called investigation centres and then resettlement of citizens, according to the operative findings of Sanski Most SJB, about 3.000 persons have moved away from the municipality since the beginning of the armed conflicts. Mainly women, children, old people. Up to the 16th of August, 1992, about 12.000 persons, mainly of Muslim, partially of Croatian ethnicity applied to Sanski Most to unregister their place of residence. In the preliminary procedure before the competent service, these persons declared they wished to leave the municipality in order to resettle, gave statements that they would either sell or give away their real estate, their movable and immovable assets, and put their movable property down on a list for transport. Again, does this to some extent accord with the information you were getting at this meeting three days afterwards?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, in terms of numbers, the one number they give me on Sanski Most was 11.000. The number on this paragraph is 12.000. Again, my reading of it would be the 11.000 was a subset of that 12.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then just very briefly, if you turn over to the next page, 8, again the reception centres in the municipality of Bosanski Novi, according to the second paragraph, on the 2nd of June, 1992, members of the army brought in citizens of Muslim ethnicity to the Mlakve stadium for their own protection. On this occasion, those brought in were not recorded but according to the SJB, about 300 persons. 5th of June set free, and then again on the 11th of June, members of the army from the area of the municipality quartered and provided security for 652 men of Muslim ethnicity fit for military service. So again, Mr. Kirudja, does that accord with all these reports you'd been getting about the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seek clarification. I always refer to that as the football field. It's the first time I see a local name for it. I assume Mlakve is the name. I've never seen this document before. I assume it is the football field, correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think I'm entitled to say you're right in that assumption?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Since I've always referred to as the football field, the numbers in that paragraph do tally in one respect. You see they are talking about 300 persons there plus a few others. The Danish report that you cited earlier counted through their binoculars and gave an estimate of 350 people in the field. So those numbers are roughly speaking in the same ballpark figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then again, resettlement of citizens, if you look, please, at the top of page 9, 13th -- 12th and 13th of May, 500 moved out, 3.500 citizens of Muslim ethnicity left on the 9th of June in the direction of Doboj. Now that would appear to accord with your 5.000 who went but it's considerably more. And then we see pursuant to the decision on the voluntary resettlement of citizens of the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and the order of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Novi on the criteria for voluntary resettlement, 5.680 persons with proper documents left the municipality on the 23rd of July, 1992, and emigrated with the assistance of UNPROFOR, and the UNHCR. Now, from what you tell us, that's a considerable underestimate?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but with one understanding, even at the beginning, they too talked about 5.000, and on these documents, 5.680 but when they actually tried to effect this evacuation, you wouldn't be surprised that the convoy was joined by various groups en route and swelled the numbers to 9.000. It wouldn't be correct to read all of them from Bosanski Novi at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes, thank you. And then finally, please, could you look at one last document from Prijedor, Exhibit P1379?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We just look, please, at page 2 of that document, which is undated -- no, I'm sorry, it isn't. 23rd of October, 1992, where according to estimates, this is about a third of the way down, after the villages which have been destroyed, according to estimates, roughly 38.000 Muslim and Croat citizens have left the municipality of Prijedor so far. Did the flow of refugees continue after these dates in August that we'd been looking at?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean after the 9.000 left?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm talking -- no. There is a meeting on the 19th of August where you're being asked to give assistance?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the UN is saying no, we won't, but did refugees continue to pass through your sector?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then just this part, if you look at the top of page 3, as time goes by, one can feel that both the official authorities and citizens themselves are relaxing under the impression that with the departure of the Muslims and Croats, everything has been accomplished. From your discussions with the mayors that you were dealing with, the Serb mayors, what impression did you get of their attitude towards getting rid of the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, in an overall impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had developed the perception from them that the enormity of their action was something they were either deliberately understating or actually didn't see it that way. They did not really see the enormity of it. And I have used elsewhere the word there seemed to be a measure of "naivete" involved in it, but incongruously related to a meticulous approach and a determination to accomplish it on the other hand. So no matter what we said, they were going to achieve this. It was more like somebody was -- an example Dvor, the first mayor says one thing, he is removed by June, his deputy comes up and is almost like a repeating verbatim what the previous mayor was saying. Then you go to Bosanski Novi. You hear identical language, almost like they are all reading from a script. It doesn't matter that they were meeting people like me and my colleagues from outside the area and saying to them, this thing is -- I'm looking for the good word. This thing has enormous implication for what you are doing. They discounted that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Thank you. That document can go. There was just one thing again I'm afraid I missed before the 19th of August. For this I think you'll need to check your diary. On the 12th of August, did you have yet another meeting with the -- Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did he want you to take out more non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there also present somebody called Mr. Deganovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was SDS representative from Bosanska Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there another SDS representative from Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanski side of Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also was there a representative of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was Mr. Saflic, Murid Saflic, representative of the Muslims wishing to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Deganovic, in fact, tell you, the SDS man, about the 5.000 people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My original text has an extra zero in error for the numbers with regard to Bosanska Kostajnica. It's not 5.000, it's 500 so he did and there were 164 families which translates to roughly to 500 persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And did he say anything else about that? About why they wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The language again was typical, like the other two Muslims on the other side, on the other meetings we alluded to, the majority want to move to Western Europe, to join relatives. First afraid to move but after the Bosanski Novi movement, they now came out wishing to move, in short the news that the Muslims had left Bosanski Novi triggered the wish of these other people to leave from Bosanska Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Pasic also tell you something about Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who? Did who tell me what?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic. I tell you what, it may be an error. Can you tell us if anything was said about Krupa?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. Yeah. Mr. Pasic began his address to me, referring to a delegation from Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa, and Prijedor to our civil police. That is the UN civil police. They had already approached them. And he went on to make a number of points. Do you want me to list them now? Because they are found in some meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime I need to leave the courtroom for a minute. --- Break taken at 12.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, we lost somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to wait for Judge Taya because it seems that I triggered -- the courtroom is -- they need to reinstall the heating or reactivate it. It's out of order today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid that Ms. Gustin was also complaining about it but I was saying it's okay. At least everybody stays awake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, sorry about that, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, you were just about to tell us, you said Mr. Pasic set out a number of things. Could you just tell us what he said?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are four elements noted in a full page and I will start with the first one. He began by summarising that before the war, there lived Muslims and Serbs lived in Bosanska Krupa in the proportions of 30 per cent Serbs, 70 per cent Muslims. Now Serbs moved to the left bank of the Una and Muslims to the right. 2. In terms of bullets, the reasons for Muslims leaving Bosanska Krupa, he gave them as, first, Serbs didn't want to conquer Muslim land for the Serbian Republic of BH. He asked that the message be conveyed that Serbs don't want to conquer Cazin region. This is the typical language of what we call Bihac pocket, Cazin region. He appealed for Muslims to find a peaceful solution by dividing the land. The world, he claimed, does not understand why Muslims want to leave voluntarily. It is because of economic and political reasons. Muslim position is economically weaker than Serbs because their livelihood was based on trade. Muslims also quote, "Are puppets of the SDA." And they have realised they were cheated by their political leaders. They realised that it is now impossible to live side by side with the Serbs. The political defeat is also linked with their military defeat, meaning Muslims, military defeat. Due to these two factors, it is obvious that Muslims were not secure. It's obvious that the Muslims did not accept their obligations. The constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina gives some rights and obligations to all citizens. One obligation is to defend their country, and Muslims would not fulfil this obligation and won't defend their country. If the Serbian side is not respected, there could be massive deaths on both sides. If we are left to resolve this matter by ourselves, we will resolve the matter very quickly. For example, there are 7.000 Serb refugees from Croatia in Bosanski Novi. The world did not condemn their plight.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When he said to you, "If we are left to resolve the matter by ourselves, we will resolve it very quickly," what did you understand him to mean?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I didn't go or delve into the details on that. What I understood and the reason I didn't delve in it, I explained this morning, and it coupled with the last sentence I read, there are 7.000 Serbs settled here. We can do did ourselves and we'll go about doing it the way we have done it before. That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think there were discussions during the meeting about the situation in Bosanska Kostajnica but I just want to deal with this: Did the mayor of Dvor say something about the evacuation of the persons from Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I note here -- just one paragraph, and it says, from the mayor of Dvor, "We went through hell during the last evacuation. We are not prepared to let refugees pass through Dvor again. Now we have to decide what to do with the Muslims, Serbs, one alternative is to leave them in their destiny. Repeat. I hope the refugees will not cross into Dvor."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say he said now we have to decide what to do with the Muslims, Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a shortcut for me to say what we as Serbs are going to do with the Muslims, the relationship, Muslim-Serb relationship.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And did the Muslim representatives say anything after that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He began to say that, to refer to the role of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He referred to them being in a war situation, meaning the Muslims, and that this is a war between the three nationalities in Bosnia, and referring to fear of reprisals each time Serbs are killed in the confrontation line. Serbs have helped prevent such reprisals. This is an allusion to -- he was very careful to always give certain deference to the Serbs to appear not to criticise, at least in our presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today's movement of population should not be considered as ethnic cleansing. He actually did want to make us understand, oh, we are not calling it ethnic cleansing but a few minutes before, he had called it a conflict of ethnic people and that each time the Serbs are killed in the confrontation line, we fear for our life. So there was this mixed messages he was trying to send to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, now I don't think anything else on that meeting but I'd like you just in respect of what you were told about Krupa, to have a look again at a report that was prepared by the Serbs, the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's not yet been exhibited but it's disclosure number 2.58. And it was on the list, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I take it that this will be 1649?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour does, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you turn to page 5, please, Mr. Kirudja, in this document? And if we look at the third paragraph on that page, "The War Presidency made an assessment of the situation and took the only feasible and appropriate decision at the time regarding the Muslim population that remained in enclaves in the Serbian territory on the right bank of the Una. First came the decision on the surrender of arms in all Muslim areas in order to free some of the units of the Serbian Territorial Defence which were maintaining a blockade of Muslim villages. This decision was very poorly implemented. No agreement was reached in the Ostruznica and Bodic area. The weak response or total disregard of Muslims to the call for surrender of arms and Alija's threat that Krupa must become green whatever the cost forced the War Presidency of the Serbian municipality to offer the Muslims two options: They could organise themselves and with our guarantees and full protection move out to the destination of their transfer, or this would be done by military means. All Muslim villages in the central regions accepted the temporary transfer provided they could take along all their movable property. The Muslim areas of Ostruznica, Bodic, and on the right bank of the Una the areas of Otoka and Crkvina were an exception and had to be dealt with militarily. You are all well aware of the outcome and manner in which this was carried out. The war chronicle of Krupa will treat this topic in more detail. The main reasons for adopting the decision on the temporary transfer of the populations were the physical safety of the Muslim people and the historically proven and confirmed nobility and kindness of Serbs who do not have a propensity for crimes and genocide. Circumstances at the time in which diplomacy still prevailed and there was still a flicker of hope the problems with Muslims and Croats or more precisely with the mujahedin and Ustashas could be resolved through negotiations and so on and so forth. Now, was there any suggestion in what were you being told by Mr. Pasic that this -- there had been a threat of military action if the Muslims didn't move?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic put it in a summary conclusion in our discussion. Both in the last meeting I referred to and the first one I met when I was probing him about the voluntary nature. He simply put it this way: The Muslims are operating from a military weakness. The converse of that statement is we are militarily stronger than they are. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You can put that document away. Now, can we look, please, at the next situation report you produced in September, which is -- was document 38 -- is document 38. It's already -- I'm told it's P1679 already in fact. So it's already been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I can say I will very definitely finish today, probably a bit earlier than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this was a special sit-rep that we can see, Mr. Kirudja, which in fact the first paragraph says is an addendum to the presumably the normal sit-rep and is entirely devoted to issues around the border which remains a continuing source of pressure for the sector. And apparently there had been a visit to that sector by General Nambiar and Mr. Thornberry to Topusko, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also Mr. Goulding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Goulding.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Goulding being whom?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of the United Nations peacekeeping operations at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you divide the border, as you've explained to us on a number of occasions, B, being the second segment separates the Bosnian opstinas of Novi, Dubica from the Krajina opstinas of Dvor and Kostajnica. Both sides of the border are controlled by Serbs of respectively the Republic of Serbian BH and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which is thus a nominal international border segment. Just dealing briefly with that, did there appear to be any real division between the RSK and the other side of the border in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: None. That was something we repeated over to try to underscore there was none.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if we can, I think leave the first few paragraphs and go to what you describe in paragraph 9 as the all-Serbian border segment? The second border segment separates two territories controlled by Serbs within the DanBat area of operation and then you list again the five Bosnian opstinas of Novi, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Banja Luka and Bosanska Dubica within which the phenomenon of ethnic cleansing has been noted. So by this stage, September, you're using that expression, ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It became clear, loud and clear. There was no need to beat around. This was a cleansing of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then you deal with the crossings and at the bottom of that paragraph 9, through the border also pass a traffic of commercial trucks to from Belgrade through the Serbian corridor opened in July with the support of the TDF troops, militia from Krajina, commanded by Milan Martic, now General Martic. And then in paragraph 10, along this border segment, refugees attempt en masse to cross to Sector North to Karlovac or other destinations in Europe. A stream of individuals arrives daily at Dvor via Novi from Prijedor and Sanski Most seeking refuge. UN CIVPOL estimates that between 30 and 50 such persons per day cross the border into Dvor. The trend during the last few weeks suggests an increase in the number of individuals that enter the sector seeking protection and assistance. And then you explain the problems this is causing to the police, the DanBat forces, and the local authorities don't appear to want to assume responsibility. Paragraph 11, the continuing flow of refugees is a destabilising factor in the area and you set out what the obvious reasons are. The number of refugees and displaced persons, the number of refugees and displaced persons passing through the sector continues to increase, the last transit of 7.000 refugees organised by UNHCR was on July the 22nd. Is that again the Novi or is it a different one?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a mistake. It should have been 9.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Subsequently a policy decision was adopted to the effect that the UN will not participate in any organised convoys rooted in the practice of ethnic cleansing. Nevertheless it is estimated that there may be more than 30.000 persons from flash points in the area within the second segment of the border as described above. If that number were to be transferred it is estimated that up to 200.000 persons are at risk and may have to be similarly evacuated. And then you talk about a coordination meeting discussing how to prevent this but you state at the bottom of the paragraph, essentially this was not a humanitarian but a political issue. And then talk about contingency matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm going to move to the last two documents so perhaps it would be convenient to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll have a 25 minute break and resume soon after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do feel they've put the heating on at full blast, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, could you be shown now please what was your document 41?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's not it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become 1650, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes but he's been given the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The front should look like this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 41?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm told by Ms. Gustin it will be P1684.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, that is another one of your, as we can see, a sit-rep, addressed to Mr. Thornberry, and did it go to Mr. Andreev again?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can see it's addressed to Mr. Thornberry, but then under -- on the front page does it say info?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is for information purposes to Victor Andreev and Jenny Pearson [phoen]. These were my counterparts in Sector South, Knin and in Belgrade at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. If we go then to the first page, you refer to the sit-rep immediate preceding it and then says this sit-rep continues the focus on issues around the border previously reported in the addendum to the sit-rep number 5 which we just looked at. Again you divide up the border and then in paragraph 4, increasingly desperate and numerous refugees from Serbian controlled Northern Bosnia have been left with no choice but to flee northwards into the UNPA. In the last four and a half days, more than 300 refugees were under DanBat protection in Dvor and 17 in Kostajnica. Then you deal with the rest. The Muslim refugees in the UNPA unfortunately find that they have moved from one hostile Serb controlled territory to another. They have to remain in transit through the UNPA even for a couple of days. Then you deal with the resistance of the Croatian authorities and in paragraph 5, the Muslims in recent weeks having resorted to bold and clandestine attempts to break out of the complete blockade. I want to go, please, straight to the fourth page where you deal with what's called the Serbian alliance in Krajina and Bosnia on which aspect you touched just before the break. Paragraph 11. As we have stated in the preceding sit-reps a nominal international border divides the Serb controlled opstinas of Dvor and Kostajnica in Krajina from the Serb controlled opstinas of Novi and Dubica across the River Una. Beyond these two or three other opstinas, Prijedor, Sanski Most and Banja Luka, in Northern Bosnia, which fall under the so-called Republic of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina. The two Serbian republics, economically depend on a corridor linking them with Serbia and Montenegro. There is also a growing evidence of a common military strategy or alliance in this regard. And observing the military structure on the ground, there are signs that Banja Luka may be exercising a balance of military power over Knin in a way analogous to the power exercised by Belgrade prior to the proclamation of a new federal Yugoslavia. The present supreme military commander in Knin is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Reportedly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Reportedly from Banja Luka while the previous one is said to be shuttling between the two capitals. Further, we have noticed the tendency of certain local authorities here to periodically retreat to Banja Luka or Belgrade at critical times. Now, can we deal -- split that. The military signs that there was control being exercised or -- I'm sorry the balance of military power from Banja Luka, where were you getting that information from?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sentence following that actually contains the answer to your question. We were tracing who was commanding, where they were going, and that basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as to the tendency of certain local authorities here to periodically retreat to Banja Luka or Belgrade at critical times, in your dealings with the political authorities, the local ones, did you get any impression that they were -- as to what their powers were to take decisions?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak directly with regard to the sector, because I was in daily arms length relationship with them. Every opstina that was part of that sector had two inter-weaved power structure, the military side and the civil side. The military side we have spoken at length. On the civil side, there were mayors, the so-called mayors of opstina A, B or C, who also had the police, the chief of police for opstina A, B or C. This group had the least influence in a way. They were on the other hand the most heard about political issues like we won't live together with the Serbs -- with the other non-Serbs. They were the most expressive when it comes to what was going on, even militarily, explaining it out, the military side normally didn't give -- were not given to giving speeches. So much of the political drive, most of the explanation was coming from the civil side of the structure. Most of the action on the other hand was taking place on the military side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say they had a tendency to retreat to Banja Luka. To do what? Or Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to think of -- again I was speaking about mayors and other people located in the sector. They were surrounded on the confrontation line by the Croats, in the direction of Karlovac, Sisak and Zagreb. Another way of putting it too, they were also blockaded themselves. We didn't mention that, the Serbs, were blockaded in that sense, economically they can't go out and they couldn't get their fuel for example. They couldn't get most normal things, because of the war the electricity was not working, because things had been broken up -- broken down and without the political -- the grid, electrical grid, normal things weren't working like water because they were all pumped. So in a way, there was a situation of shortages even for the Serbs. So for them to redress that they had to get out somehow and that's the corridor that took them to Banja Luka or Belgrade for the purposes of redressing shortages in normal, every day economic life.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In dealing with the mayors of these local areas, such as Novi, Kostajnica, Dvor, did they ever say to you or did you ever get the impression that they had to take instructions from their superiors?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that they all seemed to replicate each other in the same language was a very good indication that, if you think of it like a choir, they were all singing from a sheet that was passed around.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And, sorry? Can you just --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there was very little situations where they would deviate from that, from that -- whatever was politically correct, and we can go into the details of that. You could find hardly anybody who would deviate from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And that led you to believe what? I'm sorry to have you ask you this but we need to have it stated clearly for the terms of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were the Serbs inside the sector, that script, that choreography pointed at Knin as a centre of coordination of authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are in the Bihac areas we mentioned, outside the Bihac pocket, then I mentioned point us to Banja Luka but mostly Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Then in paragraph 12, as noted by Lord Owen and Mr. Cyrus Vance during their recent visit to Banja Luka, the practice of ethnic cleansing appears to continue unabated. Had you actually spoken to Lord Owen and Mr. Vance?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity of spending almost a day and a half with these two gentlemen, as we met in Maslenica and drove for the trip seven or eight hours. They spent the evening with us in Topusko. We debriefed them. We chatted and basically had enough time to speak to both of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then the remainder of this report lists the various refugees who have arrived, and then if you go to the next page, the humanitarian agencies, in paragraph 17, you state, given the present situation, it seems entirely reasonable to establish at least one UNHCR office in Dvor and another in Prijedor. This would make it possible to coordinate the necessary preventive action in Bosnia, in the triangle Prijedor-Bosanski Novi-Kostajnica-Dubica and assist or advise the refugees who attempt daily to cross the border into the UNPA. And I don't think we need trouble with the rest of this report. Thank you. I think we said that was going to be 1684. Yeah. And then the final document, please, that I would like to you look at is document number 44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this will become?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1685, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's not a particularly clear copy. I think is it dated December, possibly the 2nd of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, that's what it looks like in my copy. 02.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's from you, isn't it, Mr. Kirudja? We can just make that out, from C. Kirudja, Sector North, to Mr. Thornberry. The subject a group of 600 to 800 refugees from Trnopolje, message, our brief telephone conversation on the above-mentioned subject, information was relayed to us from UNHCR in Banja Luka to the effect that 600 to 800 refugees from Trnopolje are headed for Bosanski Novi with the intention of crossing into Sector North. They are?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of a group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Part of a group, about 3.000 allegedly detained in Trnopolje and is it partially evacuated?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By the ICRC to Croatia a couple of weeks ago. And heaven only knows what the rest of this says, something about Dvor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in Dvor where the refugees intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To enter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Intend to come, remains, is that remains hostile to Muslim refugees?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: UNPROFOR units get the idea?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour's copy must be much better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No it's not good, it's not at all. I mean -- I would suggest that you let the witness himself try and decipher it. Probably he's in a better condition than all of us put together. If you can read it out, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, UNPROFOR units are not in a condition to accommodate them in such numbers, nor guarantee them all the necessary security measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Prolong the stay?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think this is really isn't it, I think we perhaps, this is the nuts and bolts of how to deal with this?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it is because of the reason why you can't read it, it was typed on a teletype as opposed to the normal typewriter written reports that you read.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Just this on this document, were you aware that or had anybody informed you that they were closing this camp at Trnopolje and this was the last of the --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the last ones named in the list of what I call concentration camps, and they had come one night, one evening, in a very stressful conditions and they were being shuttled between Dvor and -- Dvor and Kostajnica areas where the Danish contingency were. So I was in touch with the UNHCR all that evening trying to ensure that they were eventually allowed to cross out, and it was very tense because as they were loaded in trucks, Danish trucks, to try to contain the situation, there was also Serbian authorities trying to collect them in their own holding places. So we had an all night of cat and mouse games with -- wherein we didn't want to release them. We wanted them out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you now recall whether this was a mixed group, in other words men, women and children, or --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The circumstances were such that we were not in a position to deal with them that way. Once they were put there, it was at night, it was raining, I remember, and it was very difficult to deal with the situation other than make sure that they crossed safely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, thank you very much indeed. That's all that I ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kirudja, you are now going to face Mr. Ackerman, who will be cross-examining you. Mr. Ackerman is the lead counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin. Mr. Ackerman, do you prefer to come forward or to stay where you are?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will come up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you need any help, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've got about 25 minutes. We'll work through as much of this as we can, and continue tomorrow. You began your testimony on Monday with questions about the state of mind that you had when you first were assigned to this mission in former Yugoslavia and Croatia, specifically you were asked about whether you went there with any preconceived notions, any biases anything of that nature. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And my recollection is that you basically said that absolutely not, you went there with a completely open mind, that you didn't know anything about what was going on, you basically didn't know the difference between Serbs and Croats and Muslims and Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats and all of those things?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially I replied to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There came a time rather quickly though, after you had arrived in Sector North, that you did form a bias, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Example?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll have several. The question is: Did you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you become biased shortly after arriving at Sector North? Did you become very pro-Muslim, anti-Serb?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I have a little -- a couple of loose ends I want to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. clear up and one of them is this: On Monday, you mentioned that the French and the Finnish battalions of UNPROFOR were initially located in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask Mr. Ackerman to provide the references on the transcript when he's referring to what was said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner is correct, Mr. Ackerman, but it's not the first time that Mr. Ackerman comes forward and says I'm afraid I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have not referred to any particular part of the transcript in his particular language yet but I'm about to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It I have the page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 17, line 25. I haven't got to the question yet. If you just kind of be patient, Ms. Korner, I'll get there with you, I promise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought the words "you said" meant you were about to repeat what he had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Line 17, page 17, line 25, with regard to the French and Finnish battalions of UNPROFOR, you said they soon found out it wasn't feasible for them to be there, referring to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know why it was that it was not feasible for them to be in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this question was in context about the assumption we had operated from, if you remember the question. And I mentioned as an example we had intended to have a headquarters in Sarajevo for the mission in its entirety and for the -- for the mission to be supplied by these logistics battalion from that area, Banja Luka, and I added that assumption came clearly wasn't going to be the way it was. It was assumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that was because logistics could not be supplied from the Banja Luka area, it's just not practical? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only mentioned that for a number of considerations, that was not to be the case and they were moved from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about what it was that made their presence in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not feasible to the --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't be more specific about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm changing subjects now. A different issue completely. You talked during your testimony, and we are essentially Ms. Korner on page 27, you talked during your testimony about several refugees, Muslim people, who were located at the football field in Karlovac and who wanted to cross through Sector North and go to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did these people ever tell you why it was they wanted to go to Bihac?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was that? What did they tell you why they wanted to go there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me the date and I'll tell you what they told me. Please remind me of the date again -- I believe I didn't give you that but I'll give it again. If you give me the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to try.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the 29th of --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 29th? Of April?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I gave you the response of General Ninkovic about it, what he said. Now I'll tell you. These were people who wanted to cross over from Karlovac, through Sector North, into Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that's where they come from, that is their origin and they have families and relatives there and they want to go and look for themselves what is going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn that they -- from any source, that they had been undergoing military training in Croatia and were trying to return to Bihac to join the battle on the Muslim side of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first source to indicate that was General Ninkovic himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have any sense of where they were coming from?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were coming -- a number of vehicles. They had been driving that were gathered in there. Some had number plates that were Croats, some were Austrian, I'm not sure another, but there were some licence plates which were Austrian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you conclude from that that these were people who might have been previously living and working in places like Austria and Croatia and had then become part of a training programme to return to Bihac and join the fighting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only partly to your question I could discern they were living and working outside of Bosnia. That much I could discern because they also said so. The second part of your question, whether or not somebody had trained them militarily, there was nothing in the football field situation that would make me conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you did tell us on Monday that they were virtually all military age males?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact that's what the counsel for the Prosecution asked me, whether they looked like trained people and I responded the only thing you can see is that they are mostly males and they are in good health.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's hard to tell how somebody looks if they have been militarily trained, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes you can but not always, sometimes if you got what we call a military crew cut and the other things, there are some signs but I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. You had a meeting on the 26th of May of 1992 with the mayor of Dvor, and you might want to look at your diary on that date.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, the date again?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 26 May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 26 May. Mayor of Dvor?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, the mayor of Dvor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the conversation was about 5.000 persons who wanted to leave Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what the mayor was telling you was that they wanted safe passage through Sector North for these 5.000 people who were transiting to I believe he told you primarily Austria and Germany?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you told also, I believe, that these were people who had relatives and friends in Austria and Germany who were prepared to accommodate them there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were told that they wanted to depart and that they were leaving voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th, there was -- yes, the element that they were leaving voluntarily and they were going to those two places, that was communicated to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The second request that was made at that time was that you provide an international film crew to film the transit of these people across the Serb-controlled area, specifically to document that they passed through safely?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did not remain in the Serb-controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you told us you were uncomfortable with that proposition and that in your mind something about this was not right, yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, in summary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we contrast that with these -- this group of Muslims there in that football stadium at Karlovac who seemed willing to leave there and go to Bihac in the middle of an area that was under stress, fighting, were you uncomfortable with this trying to assist them in any way to make the journey in the other direction?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The comparison you assume is the same. You want me to compare the two and I can't. For one thing in the case of the Muslims, in my meeting, there were no Muslims. I'm talking to Serbs. In the case of the football field in Karlovac, I'm not talking with an intermediary, I'm talking to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So were you talking directly with these people at the --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Football field.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Karlovac football field?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I was in the football field, among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With regard to the group from Dvor, from Novi, when you were talking to the mayor of Dvor, you asked the mayor, did you not, where this group was coming from?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were told that they were coming from their homes basically. Yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you told us or maybe it's in that document, that you were concerned because, as you said, how do people voluntarily leave the comfort of their homes and go to far away places? That didn't seem to add up?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was summarising the conclusion we reached, not how we got there. He also told me a number of things that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But that was a concern of yours, how do people voluntarily leave the comfort of their homes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And go to far away places?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After hearing a number of things from a person purportedly speaking, he -- reporting his counterpart about a group, they don't represent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what made you suspicious, though, was the proposition that people were voluntarily leaving the comfort of their homes to go to far away places?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's something --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just didn't buy that, did you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't buy that but I also said why. I also prefaced that by saying I asked the mayor to explain me, and I prefaced that with a statement, the mayor you speak convincingly about matters, and I tend to understand it when you speak for the Serbs. You are now switching that, you are speaking for the Muslims in a manner that doesn't add up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These people from Bosanski Novi were people who were living in a place, as you've already told us, which had no electricity for large parts of the time. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said they were living in a place with no electricity in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know that Bosanski Novi had no electricity, significant parts of the time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're telling me now they had no electricity?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were telling us just a moment ago about the shortages of electricity?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Throughout the whole area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Do you know that they were living where there were severe food and medicine shortages?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that your statement to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking you did you know?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know that they were people who may have been liable for conscription into military service?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was already told that by the mayor of Dvor, that they tried -- they wouldn't and they wouldn't fight.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know that these were people living just across the border from a war zone who may have had a reasonable belief that the war could cross the border and reach --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll break that question. Across the border war zone, which side of the border are you referring to as a war zone?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you were there, because the place you went had been a war zone that secretary Vance had interceded in and managed to achieve --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely I went in to tell you the war zone was on the side which was Croatian territory occupied by the Serbs. Bosanski Novi on the other side, when we arrived, it wasn't a war zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But my question was this: They were living, the people in Bosanski Novi, were living just across the border from a war zone?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, that's different.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or a previous war zone?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And might have been, probably had, a reasonable belief and concern that that war could expand across the border?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You do know that in a war zone, civilians always suffer, don't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have seen a good example of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you think it would be fair to say that these people in that situation at that time in that place were very unlikely to have been people finding much comfort in their homes during these times?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us at the beginning of your testimony Monday, just as a general proposition, we talked about it just a moment ago, that you knew virtually nothing about the situation. The question, as you went there. The question I want to ask you is: Were you briefed at all?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm coming there, just give me a minute to finish the question. Were you briefed at all before you took up that assignment about the situation you why going into?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We get briefed as part of -- we are the UN, we are representatives, we have a job to do. We do get briefed about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where did that briefing take place?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first briefing would be in our own headquarters about what it is -- what the mission is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how long did that briefing take?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall really exactly how long but first you get the documents themselves, and I read them. Then I meet with Mr. Thornberry who was then at headquarters and other people and we listen to their mission but basically, most of the briefing would be in the form of documentation. UN documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I take it then there was a second briefing after you arrived in?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long that briefing was and the nature of it and so forth?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
